occurrences.source_excerpt: Skeletal Muscles Skeletal muscles attach to bones via tendons Made up of muscle fibres, wrapped in a dense connect tissue sheath Blood supply – branches of arteries and capillary network penetrate in muscles Classification: Type I – slow-twitch fibres contract • slowly, moderate force level, resist fatigue Type II – fast twitch fibres contract rapidly, high force level, fatigue quickly Functions: Voluntary movements Posture & stability Storage of protein Heat production Joint protection

occurrences.source_excerpt: Complications of Soft Tissue Injuries Acute complications occur with soft tissue injuries: Blood vessels damage Haemorrhage - serious • internal bleeding Ischaemia - loss of blood supply to body tissues Nerves damage Direct trauma Compression due to swelling • Compartment syndrome Severe swelling within muscle • compartment (fascia) Intense pain and cut off • blood supply

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – OL for Optimal Loading Objective: To accelerate healing process • as body tissues require some loading to start healing Action: Gradual introduction of • activity & movement under proper protection Gentle manual techniques, • exercise with supports Why Important: Right amount of activity help to manage swelling with • muscle pumping Prolonged rest / • immobilization may lead to complications such as contracture

occurrences.source_excerpt: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? Compression of median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel Carpal Tunnel: U-shaped canal consists of carpal bones, with a dense fibrous tissue (Transverse Carpal Ligament) covering on top Median Nerve & Flexor Tendons of hand pass through this tunnel

occurrences.source_excerpt: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? occurrences.source_excerpt: Management of CTS Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Wrist flexor • and extensor stretches to improve flexibility. Wrist Splinting: Use splints to keep the wrist in a neutral position, especially at night, to avoid excessive flexion. • (NSAIDs) Medical Management Medications: NSAIDs to relieve pain and inflammation. Steroid Injections: Injections in the carpal tunnel to reduce • inflammation and swelling. Treat Underlying Conditions: Manage diabetes and arthritis to improve symptoms.

occurrences.source_excerpt: Management of Tennis Elbow Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Stretches for the forearm extensors to improve flexibility. Strengthening Exercises: Strengthening • exercises for the forearm and wrist muscles • once pain subsides. Manual Therapy: Techniques to reduce muscle tension and improve blood circulation. Ice Therapy: Application of ice to reduce inflammation and pain. Activity Modification: Educating patients on avoiding repetitive motions that aggravate the condition. (NSAIDs)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Management of CTS Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Wrist flexor • and extensor stretches to improve flexibility. Wrist Splinting: Use splints to keep the wrist in a neutral position, especially at night, to avoid excessive flexion. • (NSAIDs) Medical Management Medications: NSAIDs to relieve pain and inflammation. Steroid Injections: Injections in the carpal tunnel to reduce • inflammation and swelling. Treat Underlying Conditions: Manage diabetes and arthritis to improve symptoms.

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – P for Protection Objective: To prevent further damage to the injured area Action: Protect injured part from • further injury Using supports like splints, • braces, or crutches to avoid movements that could worsen the injury Why Important: Limits additional damage Stabilizes the injury Prevent further trauma other soft tissues

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 22 (PDF p. 22)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – I for Ice Objective: To reduce acute • inflammation, pain & swelling Action: Apply ice / cold pack for 15- • 20 min every 1-2 hours during first 48-72 hours after injury Ice until resting pain subsided Why Important: Constricts blood vessels, reduce blood flow to injured • area, limits swelling & bruising Immediate pain relief with pain gate theory

occurrences.source_excerpt: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? Compression of median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel Carpal Tunnel: U-shaped canal consists of carpal bones, with a dense fibrous tissue (Transverse Carpal Ligament) covering on top Median Nerve & Flexor Tendons of hand pass through this tunnel

occurrences.source_excerpt: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? Compression of median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel Carpal Tunnel: U-shaped canal consists of carpal bones, with a dense fibrous tissue (Transverse Carpal Ligament) covering on top Median Nerve & Flexor Tendons of hand pass through this tunnel

occurrences.source_excerpt: Management of CTS Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Wrist flexor • and extensor stretches to improve flexibility. Wrist Splinting: Use splints to keep the wrist in a neutral position, especially at night, to avoid excessive flexion. • (NSAIDs) Medical Management Medications: NSAIDs to relieve pain and inflammation. Steroid Injections: Injections in the carpal tunnel to reduce • inflammation and swelling. Treat Underlying Conditions: Manage diabetes and arthritis to improve symptoms.

occurrences.source_excerpt: Treatment Principle – RICE Traditional principles – RICE Rest, Ice, Compress, Elevate – POLICE Modern principles – POLICE P = Protection OL = Optimal Loading I = Ice C = Compression E = Elevation

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 20 (PDF p. 20)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – P for Protection Objective: To prevent further damage to the injured area Action: Protect injured part from • further injury Using supports like splints, • braces, or crutches to avoid movements that could worsen the injury Why Important: Limits additional damage Stabilizes the injury Prevent further trauma other soft tissues

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 21 (PDF p. 21)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – OL for Optimal Loading Objective: To accelerate healing process • as body tissues require some loading to start healing Action: Gradual introduction of • activity & movement under proper protection Gentle manual techniques, • exercise with supports Why Important: Right amount of activity help to manage swelling with • muscle pumping Prolonged rest / • immobilization may lead to complications such as contracture

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 22 (PDF p. 22)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – I for Ice Objective: To reduce acute • inflammation, pain & swelling Action: Apply ice / cold pack for 15- • 20 min every 1-2 hours during first 48-72 hours after injury Ice until resting pain subsided Why Important: Constricts blood vessels, reduce blood flow to injured • area, limits swelling & bruising Immediate pain relief with pain gate theory

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 23 (PDF p. 23)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – C for Compression Objective: To minimize swelling To provide support to injured • area Action: Apply elastic bandage or compression wrap to gently • compress injured area Avoid tight compression that restrict circulation • Why Important: Reduce fluid build up in the • tissues Reduce swelling

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 24 (PDF p. 24)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – E for Elevation Objective: To reduce swelling To promote drainage of excess fluid Action: Elevate the injured body part to above heart level for 20-30 min, several times a day, esp. first 48 hours • Why Important: Encourages venous return Reduce swelling

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 33 (PDF p. 33)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Lateral Ankle Sprain Physiotherapy Management: Follow POLICE protocol in • inflammatory phase (Day 0 – POLICE Day 6) Aircast / orthopaedic boot Elbow crutches if necessary, at least partial (PWB) weight bearing (PWB) Mobilization exercise for • ROM Strengthening exercise for • muscle strength Proprioception training Functional activity training

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 44 (PDF p. 44)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Achilles Tendon Rupture Physiotherapy Management: Early rehabilitation follow POLICE POLICE protocol in inflammatory phase Functional bracing / casting in plantar flexed position for 8-12 • weeks Protected weight-bearing with elbow crutches Mobilization exercise for ROM • for early phase, avoid stretching of Achilles Tendon at early phase Strengthening exercise for • muscle strength at later stage (typically 6 weeks later) Proprioception training Functional activity training

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 52 (PDF p. 52)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Muscle Contusion Physiotherapy Management: POLICE Early rehabilitation follow POLICE protocol in inflammatory phase (first 24-48 hours) Mobilization exercise for ROM Strengthening exercise for muscle strength once full & pain-free ROM achieved Functional activity training Sport-specific training

occurrences.source_excerpt: Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) Common occupational health problem Gradual onset of • discomfort / pain Affecting muscles, tendons, • ligaments, nerve, bursa, etc. Caused by repeated micro- • trauma over a period of time, without any single trauma: Repetitive movements Sustained postures Forceful movements Stress and undesirable working environment

occurrences.source_excerpt: Common Examples of RSI Fingers & thumbs Trigger finger Wrist Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Elbow 、 golfer's elbow( Tennis Elbow, Golfer’s Elbow Shoulders Rotator Cuff Tendinitis Neck Tension Neck Syndrome Back Low back pain

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 59 (PDF p. 59)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Common Signs & Symptoms of RSI Early symptoms include Soreness, pain, tingling & discomfort when performing the repetitive task Symptoms reduced when stop the task Common sings & symptoms if left untreated and gradual deteriorate: Burning, aching or shooting pain Swelling Stiffness Throbbing Tingling / numbness Muscle weakness Muscle cramp

occurrences.source_excerpt: General Risk Factors for RSI Work posture (esp. awkward or improper posture) work at a non-ergonomically designed workspace Heavy physical work Lifting Repetitive, labour-intensive • work prolonged use on computer, keyboard & mouse Vibration (via hand tools) Extreme low temperature Individual risk factors: Smoking High Body Mass Index (BMI) Co-morbidities

occurrences.source_excerpt: Ligaments Connective tissues that connect • bones together Made up of bundles of • collagen fibers Attached to outer covering of • bones – periosteum Blood supply – at insertion site Functions: Restrict joint motion to prevent excessive joint • movements) Stabilize joint Joint proprioception

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 6 (PDF p. 6)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Tendons Dense connective tissues that connect muscles to bones Made up of bundles of • collagen fibers Each muscle has 2 tendons: proximal & distal Blood supply – musculotendinous junction, osseotendinous junction Functions: Transfer forces from muscles to bones to produce joint motion

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury
source_pages.formatted: HHS4185J_L3_軟組織問題_Soft tissue injuries.pdf, slide 8 (PDF p. 8)

occurrences.source_excerpt: Skeletal Muscles Skeletal muscles attach to bones via tendons Made up of muscle fibres, wrapped in a dense connect tissue sheath Blood supply – branches of arteries and capillary network penetrate in muscles Classification: Type I – slow-twitch fibres contract • slowly, moderate force level, resist fatigue Type II – fast twitch fibres contract rapidly, high force level, fatigue quickly Functions: Voluntary movements Posture & stability Storage of protein Heat production Joint protection

occurrences.source_excerpt: Acute (immediate) soft tissue injuries Usually results of a single traumatic event / accident Strains: Overstretch / tear a muscle or tendon Sudden / jerky movement Sprains: Overstretch / tear a ligament Sudden / jerky movement • Contusions: A bruise with broken blood • vessels causing discolouration under the skin Forceful impact from a direct blow, fall or collision

source_pages.document_title: Lecture 3 - Orthopaedic Soft Tissue Problems: Acute Sprain and Repetitive Stress Injury

occurrences.source_excerpt: Complications of Soft Tissue Injuries Acute complications occur with soft tissue injuries: Blood vessels damage Haemorrhage - serious • internal bleeding Ischaemia - loss of blood supply to body tissues Nerves damage Direct trauma Compression due to swelling • Compartment syndrome Severe swelling within muscle • compartment (fascia) Intense pain and cut off • blood supply

occurrences.source_excerpt: Management of Tennis Elbow Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Stretches for the forearm extensors to improve flexibility. Strengthening Exercises: Strengthening • exercises for the forearm and wrist muscles • once pain subsides. Manual Therapy: Techniques to reduce muscle tension and improve blood circulation. Ice Therapy: Application of ice to reduce inflammation and pain. Activity Modification: Educating patients on avoiding repetitive motions that aggravate the condition. (NSAIDs)

occurrences.source_excerpt: POLICE – I for Ice Objective: To reduce acute • inflammation, pain & swelling Action: Apply ice / cold pack for 15- • 20 min every 1-2 hours during first 48-72 hours after injury Ice until resting pain subsided Why Important: Constricts blood vessels, reduce blood flow to injured • area, limits swelling & bruising Immediate pain relief with pain gate theory

occurrences.source_excerpt: Skeletal Muscles Skeletal muscles attach to bones via tendons Made up of muscle fibres, wrapped in a dense connect tissue sheath Blood supply – branches of arteries and capillary network penetrate in muscles Classification: Type I – slow-twitch fibres contract • slowly, moderate force level, resist fatigue Type II – fast twitch fibres contract rapidly, high force level, fatigue quickly Functions: Voluntary movements Posture & stability Storage of protein Heat production Joint protection

Wrist Splinting: Use splints to keep the wrist in a neutral position, especially at night, to avoid excessive flexion. • (NSAIDs) Medical Management Medications: NSAIDs to relieve pain and inflammation. Steroid Injections: Injections in the carpal tunnel to reduce • inflammation and swelling. Treat Underlying Conditions: Manage diabetes and arthritis to improve symptoms.
